doc.title: Chico Hamilton interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 30, 2000

title: Eight years with Lena Horne and mentor Lennie Hayton
summary: Playing for singers, learning from Hayton, Luther Henderson and Strayhorn, and being a professional.

story.theme_name: Singers and the musicians who accompanied them
story.community_name: Working with Sinatra: bands, Vegas and the Sands

blocks.x: You could just imagine seeing that you know? And I’ve had a lot of beautiful experiences playing with various — I think the most rewarding in a sense, experience that I’ve had, I spent about fifteen years playing for singers, nothing but singers. And I was with Lena Horne for eight years. And during that period with Lena Horne it took me out of the realm of just being a musician. It took me into show biz. That’s a big difference between a musician, a jazz musician, and show biz people, the whole thing. It just opened up a whole new world for me. And through that eight years we played, I played for some of the most notable people of the times during that era. And we played all over the world, things like that. And I became — her husband, Lennie Hayton, he became my mentor. And I learned a hell of a lot about music from this man. This man was a genius and a gentleman, had class, he taught me how to play chess, he taught me how to eat a lobster, things like that. Taught me how to drink cognac. No he was a good dude and we were friends. He and Luther Henderson and Billy Strayhorn were my whatever — I was the kid, they embraced me. And it was very rewarding because those things that I learned are still with me today. I try to in turn bestow this upon other younger players that come up that are on the scene today. Because be a professional you know?
It’s not as easy as it sounds.
No it’s not. But if you think in terms of being a professional, hey, you can get just like a doctor, a lawyer or anybody else. You are a professional musician.
